name: Carla Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the returns hall at a big online clothes warehouse, the day shift, seven till half three. People send back dresses and jeans and trainers, and I open the bags, check each thing for stains or tags missing, grade it, and either repack it for sale or send it to the bin pile. You'd be amazed what comes back, I once found a wedding invitation in a jacket pocket. The other half of my day I'm picking for outgoing orders when they're short-handed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the returns side because it's a bit of a puzzle, working out if a top was worn or just tried on. What wears me out is the speed and the agency temps coming and going every few weeks, so you're always training someone new. My supervisor, Dev, says my grading is still too slow, and he's right, I second-guess myself on the borderline ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, told you so, it was a bubble. At work we'd laugh about the scanner that was supposed to grade clothes by itself and never worked. Online I'd share a meme about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the normal worries stay normal. The company keeps talking about moving returns to a cheaper site two hours away, and that was happening before anyone said AI. It could still happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep putting about two hundred a month into savings, and go to the union meeting about the returns move. I've been thinking about standing as a rep, and in a calm year like that I might actually do it. Noor, my girlfriend, says I'd be good at it because I never shut up about fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. The AI news would stop, but the rumours about the move wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If returns did move two hours away, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to pick between a long commute and finding another warehouse. There are a few around the motorway junction, so I'd probably find something. It would mean starting at the bottom again on new kit, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have to fall back on right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two months of rent and bills, if we're careful. Noor earns a bit more than me at the nursery, so we'd survive a gap. I wouldn't want to test it for long.

say: I'd joke at work that the **AI grading scanner** never worked anyway.
I'd share a **meme** online rather than make a big point.
think: The real risk is the company **moving returns** to a cheaper site two hours away.
That threat **existed before AI** and wouldn't go away in a plateau.
do: Keep saving about **two hundred** a month on top of two months put by.
Stand as a **union rep** and push on the returns move.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **flat**, with the move rumours still in the air.
S0.quote: The company keeps talking about moving returns to a cheaper site two hours away, and that was happening before anyone said AI.
fieldNote: Her main worry in a plateau is **site relocation**, not technology.
She is drawn to becoming a **union rep**, rooted in her sense of fairness.
Her girlfriend Noor's **nursery wage** gives the household a small extra buffer.

steps.text: Put two hundred a month into savings
Stand for union rep in the returns hall
Keep grading returns on the day shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules. If a camera is going to grade returns instead of people, someone has to check it's fair and that we get trained for whatever's next. I'd say it at work and I'd sign petitions for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My returns job is mostly looking at things and deciding. Returns grading is checking, and checking is on that list. If the camera finally works, I'm back to just picking. Picking would last a bit longer, but the hall would need half the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dev if I could be one of the people who trains the camera system or checks what it gets wrong. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to write emails to the landlord, so I'm not scared of it. I'd also push the union to make the company pay for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but not hopeless. It feels like a change I could get ahead of if I move a bit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunita, who's done returns for nine years and is the fastest grader we have. Her whole skill is the thing the camera does. She doesn't read English well, so a course on a screen would be hard for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move early, but you also said you change when things are proven. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I won't jump on day one, but once I see the camera working on the next line over, I'm not going to wait for a letter. That's about as early as I get.

say: I'd say a camera grading returns needs **rules** and fair checks.
I'd sign **petitions** for company-paid training for people moved off grading.
think: Returns grading is **checking work**, so it's first in line for AI.
Picking would last longer, but the hall would need **half the people**.
do: Ask Dev to let me **train or check** the new camera system.
Push the union so the company **pays for courses**.
Keep using AI on my phone so the new tools feel **familiar**.
feel: **Nervous** but not hopeless, as if she could get ahead by moving early.
S1.quote: Returns grading is checking, and checking is on that list. If the camera finally works, I'm back to just picking.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **grading** is thinking work exposed to AI before picking.
Her worry for her colleague Sunita shows concern about **language barriers** in retraining.
She resolves her contradiction: she moves once she **sees proof** nearby.

steps.text: Volunteer to check errors from the AI grading camera
Press the union for company-paid courses
Keep two months of bills in the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government has to step in, with money for people while they retrain. I'd post about it, which I hardly ever do. At work I'd be the one handing out union forms at break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grading goes almost straight away, because a thinking AI can look at a stain as well as I can. Then around 2031 the robots arrive for picking and packing. So I'd have maybe two years of picking left after grading goes, and then I'd be thirty-two with nothing on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut our takeaways and look at a cheaper flat when the lease ends in spring. I'd sign up for the childcare course Noor keeps telling me about, evenings, so I'm qualified before the robots come. I'd also stand as rep for sure, because people will need someone in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. My stomach drops when I picture the hall with no people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched Noor at the nursery. Nobody wants a robot wiping a toddler's nose, so I'd do the childcare course while I still have a wage. It's not well paid, but it's people. And I'm good with kids, my nieces are always on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might be living on her wage for a year while I train. Then I'd ask if we can still afford the holiday in the summer, and I already know the answer. She'd say we'll manage, she always does.

say: I'd say the **government** must pay people to live while they retrain.
I'd hand out **union forms** at break and actually post online.
think: **Grading** goes almost at once, then robots take **picking** around 2031.
At thirty-two I'd have **nothing on paper** to show for my work.
do: Cut **takeaways** and look for a cheaper flat when the lease ends.
Start an evening **childcare course** before the robots arrive.
Stand as **union rep** to speak for the hall.
feel: **Scared**, with her stomach dropping at the thought of an empty hall.
S2.quote: Nobody wants a robot wiping a toddler's nose, so I'd do the childcare course while I still have a wage.
fieldNote: She has a **specific escape**: childcare, modelled on her girlfriend's job.
She sees a **two-step loss**: grading to AI first, picking to robots later.
She would rely on Noor's **income** for a year and feels the weight of that.

steps.text: Cancel takeaways and find a cheaper flat at lease end
Enrol in an evening childcare course
Stand as union rep for the returns hall
Live on Noor's nursery wage during training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's plan it properly this time. The company should tell us now which jobs are going and when. I'd say that to Dev and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grading would go around 2031, and picking about three years after, so maybe 2034. That's enough time to get a qualification part-time without wrecking our money. I wouldn't be calm, but I'd have a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the childcare course next September, one evening a week, and keep working full time. I'd keep saving and I'd use AI more to help me study, because my reading and writing aren't great. And I'd keep pushing the union to get a proper redundancy deal agreed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, but I can breathe. Five years is a deadline, not a cliff. I'd have time to get a childcare qualification part-time without wrecking our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use AI to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask it to explain the bits I don't get in simpler words, like it's talking to me and not to a professor. I've done that once already with a letter from the council. It's useful when you left school early like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing it while working. Coming home from a shift and opening a textbook is hard when your feet ache. Noor would have to keep me at it.

say: I'd say five years means the company should **tell us now** which jobs go.
I'd raise it with my supervisor Dev and **anyone who listens**.
think: Grading goes around **2031** and picking around **2034**.
That's enough time for a **part-time qualification** without wrecking our money.
do: Start a **childcare course** one evening a week from next September.
Use AI to **explain study material** in simpler words.
Push for an early **redundancy deal** through the union.
feel: **Tight in the chest** but able to breathe, as with a deadline.
S3.quote: Five years is a deadline, not a cliff. I'd have time to get a childcare qualification part-time without wrecking our money.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **workable plan**.
She already uses AI to **decode letters** and would use it to study.
**Fatigue** after shifts is the main threat to her plan.

steps.text: Start a one-evening-a-week childcare course next September
Use the AI app to explain course reading
Push the union for an early redundancy deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we don't. I'd push for the company and the government to start training people now. Online I'd probably share articles about it now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to do this properly. Grading by 2036, robots by 2039, and I'd be forty by then. I could finish a childcare qualification, work a few years in a nursery and still have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at courses but probably not start, I'd want to see how the first AI grading goes. I'd keep saving the two hundred a month. Noor and I might start talking about kids, because a decade is long enough to plan a family around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There's a lot of road ahead, but I can see where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the course sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our hall got the AI grading camera early and it actually worked. Seeing Sunita moved off returns would do it. That would be my alarm bell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change anything about kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it makes me want them sooner, while I'm still working somewhere steady. Or maybe it makes me want to wait until I've retrained. Noor and I would argue about that one, nicely.

say: I'd say a decade is a **gift if used**, and push for training to start now.
I'd share **articles** online every now and then.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty, with time to qualify and work in a nursery.
A decade gives me time to **retrain properly** without draining savings.
do: Research **childcare courses** but wait to see AI grading first.
Start talking with Noor about **having kids**.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with a long road but a clear direction.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we don't.
fieldNote: With a decade, her **steady** nature shows: she watches before acting.
Her **trigger** would be a colleague moved off returns.
The timeline feeds into **family plans** with her girlfriend.

steps.text: Keep saving two hundred a month
Watch how AI grading works before enrolling
Plan with Noor when to try for children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to finish a course while working, so I'd be out of grading with nothing new to go to. What would help is money to live on while I train, and a company that has to tell people early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the agency temps. Agency temps will go first in every one of these pictures, and nobody will even count them. If you're writing this up, I'd want them in it.

headlineQuote: Agency temps will go first in every one of these pictures, and nobody will even count them.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old returns grader** at an online clothes warehouse, still slow on borderline items.
She is **progressive** and wants rules, union deals and paid retraining rather than blaming the technology.
Her plan B is **childcare**, inspired by her girlfriend Noor's nursery job.
She sees **grading** going to AI before **picking** goes to robots, and plans around that gap.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** in a plateau to **alarmed** if AGI comes by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she couldn't finish a course before grading disappears.
whatWouldHelp: **Living money** while retraining and early warning from the company about cuts.
